title: Caught on Video: Sperm Whales Team Up to Help a Mom Give Birth
summary: It really does take a village to raise a baby—even for whales! Scientists have captured the first-ever video of a sperm whale giving birth, and it shows something incredible: a whole team of whales helping the mom. The footage was recorded in 2023 off the island of Dominica in the Caribbean Sea. A marine biologist named David Gruber and his team from Project CETI were in the right place at the right time with their drones. They filmed the entire 34-minute birth. A group of 10 sperm whales surrounded the mother, named Rounder. After the calf came out, the helpers took turns gently lifting the newborn to the surface. Why? Because a baby sperm whale can't float or swim well at first—it would sink without help! The whales held it up for hours until it could swim on its own. Even more surprising, the helpers weren't all family. Some were from a different whale family group that doesn't usually hang out with Rounder's group. But they all worked together. The researchers also recorded the whales' sounds, called codas. They noticed that a special coda was used more often during the birth, almost like a signal. Afterward, when some pilot whales showed up, the sperm whales changed their sounds again—maybe to warn each other. This amazing video shows just how cooperative and caring sperm whales can be, especially during one of the most important moments of their lives.
why_it_matters: Learning how whales help each other during birth shows us how important teamwork is in the animal kingdom, and reminds us to protect these intelligent creatures.

background_read: Sperm whales are the largest toothed animals on Earth and live in tight family groups called pods.
Dominica, a small Caribbean island, is one of the few places where sperm whales live all year round, making it a favorite spot for researchers.
David Gruber (a marine biologist) and his Project CETI team use drones and underwater microphones to study whale communication.
Article_Structure: WHO: Mother sperm whale Rounder, helper whales, and scientist David Gruber's team
WHAT: They captured the first-ever birth video, showing whales lifting the calf and changing sounds
WHERE: In the Caribbean Sea near the island of Dominica
WHY: To reveal how sperm whales work together and communicate during important life events

perspectives.description: The video shows wonderful teamwork even across different whale families, highlighting the social intelligence of whales.
Since sperm whales are endangered, understanding their behaviors helps create better protections for them and their habitats.
This rare footage opens new questions about whale communication, like whether codas have meanings similar to language.
